title: Rocket the Raccoon to the Rescue: How Fifth Graders Are Easing First-Day Fears
summary:
The first day of school can be terrifying for a five-year-old. New building, new faces, and mom and dad waving goodbye at the gate. But at Micheltorena Street Elementary in Los Angeles, a heartwarming tradition is turning those tears into smiles.

Principal Nichole Sakellarion noticed 11 years ago that her youngest students struggled with the transition to elementary school. So she created a program that welcomes kindergarteners a day early, pairing them with fifth-grade "toolbox coaches" who mentor them throughout the year.

On the big day, the coaches take the little ones by the hand at the front gates and walk them to their teachers. Ten-year-old Noemi Ulloa remembers feeling shy and overwhelmed when she first started at this school. Now she's determined to help others. "As a toolbox coach, I think I can help kindergartners harness their emotions," she said.

Fellow coach Gerald Gomez-Reina teaches his younger buddies practical tools for managing big feelings. He explains techniques like taking deep breaths or using the "garbage can" method — "when you throw away feelings, if you get sad or mad." He even brought his favorite stuffed animal, Rocket the Raccoon, to comfort any nervous newcomers.

The results speak for themselves. On the actual first day, parents lined the chain-link fence, tears streaming down their faces as they waved goodbye. But Sakellarion marveled, "Almost no tears today from the kindergarteners! That's amazing."

This tradition is part of a nationwide back-to-school wave, with about 54 million students returning to classrooms. At Will Rogers Elementary in Oklahoma, some families participate in a "bike bus," riding together to school once a week to avoid traffic and have fun.

But at Micheltorena, the focus is on emotional support. By pairing older and younger students, the school creates a community where everyone looks out for each other. It's a simple idea with powerful results: a first day filled with high-fives, hand-holding, and the comforting presence of a stuffed raccoon.
why_it_matters: This article is about more than one school's first day: it is a reminder that transitions feel scary at any age, and that small acts of kindness from older students can change how a whole school feels. A middle schooler could use the same idea to help younger students or new classmates feel included.

background_read: Micheltorena Street Elementary is a public school in Los Angeles.

Starting kindergarten is one of the first major transitions in school life: small children must leave their parents, learn new routines, and share a large building with much older kids, so tears and anxiety are common.
Many schools across the United States use buddy or mentor programs that pair older students with younger ones.

The idea behind them comes from social-emotional learning, which teaches children to notice and name their feelings and to practice strategies like deep breathing or imagining they can throw bad feelings away.
When fifth graders are called toolbox coaches, the toolbox metaphor means they have practical coping tools, just as a worker has a toolkit for fixing problems.
Research on school climate suggests that a familiar older face can make a younger child feel safer and reduce behavior problems later.

├─ WHO: fifth graders mentor kindergarteners; Noemi Ulloa and Gerald Gomez-Reina are coaches.
├─ WHY: Sakellarion noticed 11 years ago that youngest students struggled with the transition.
└─ HOW: coaches hold hands at the gate, walk kids to teachers, and show emotional tools.
EVIDENCE: Parents cried, but almost no kindergarteners did; the principal quotes the result.
CONTEXT: A nationwide back-to-school wave includes about 54 million students; an Oklahoma school runs a bike bus.
CONCLUSION: Pairing older and younger students builds a caring community.

perspectives.description: Kindergarteners get a familiar older face at the gate, while fifth-grade coaches build leadership skills and learn that their empathy can solve real problems.

perspectives.perspective: Not every school can easily copy this
perspectives.description: The program depends on teachers organizing schedules, training fifth graders, and keeping the mentoring going all year. Schools with less time or money may find it harder, even though the idea is simple.

First-day tears are a normal stress reaction to an unfamiliar environment. Pairing new students with older mentors is a low-tech way to give kids a sense of safety before they have to cope on their own.
The same toolbox-coach approach could be expanded to other grade transitions, such as students entering middle school, where anxiety is often just as high even when tears are hidden.
